messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fisherman
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Babies): Babies, Public Transport: Bus riding, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable
  Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room, Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

Vignette:
Aleksander Nowak is a 26-year-old Polish-American fisherman who presented for psychological assessment approximately fourteen months after surviving a prolonged episode of politically motivated torture while visiting relatives in a region of Eastern Europe experiencing civil unrest. He is married, lives in a coastal town in the Pacific Northwest, and works on a commercial fishing vessel. His PCL-5 score of 37 places him in a clinically significant range, and the picture he describes across several intake sessions is one of a young man whose inner life has been fundamentally reorganised around the expectation of danger.

The event itself occurred over the course of roughly thirty-six hours. Aleksander had been detained by a paramilitary faction, held in a bare concrete room, and subjected to repeated physical assaults and periods of prolonged stress positioning — his arms wrenched behind him, his body forced into a kneeling posture on a hard floor for hours at a time. He was blindfolded for much of the ordeal. At one point a guard entered the room carrying an infant — a detail Aleksander still cannot fully explain — and the baby's crying filled the space during one of the worst episodes of the detention. He was eventually released without formal charge and returned to the United States within weeks, visibly injured and largely silent about what had happened.

In the months that followed, Aleksander found that the world had become a different kind of place. The baby's crying, which had been the acoustic backdrop to some of the most severe moments of his captivity, now reached him anywhere — in the supermarket, in a neighbour's yard, through a thin apartment wall. Each time, something in his body responded before his mind could intervene. His muscles would tighten, his breath would shallow, and he would feel, with terrible physical certainty, that his arms were being pulled back behind him and his knees were pressing into concrete. The pain was not metaphorical. It arrived in his shoulders and his kneecaps as something real and present, and with it came a fury so intense he sometimes had to leave the room. He had come to believe that this rage meant something was permanently broken in him — that the person who came back from Eastern Europe was not the same man his wife had married.

His work on the fishing vessel presented its own difficulties. The boat's confined quarters meant that Aleksander was rarely able to position himself with his back to a solid surface while facing outward, and on days when the crew moved around him unpredictably he found himself cataloguing every object within reach — a filleting knife left on a crate, a gaff hook hanging near the stern — not as tools of his trade but as things that could be used against him or, he admitted quietly, by him. He had begun taking the bus to the harbour each morning, but after several weeks he found he could no longer tolerate the experience of sitting in a moving vehicle surrounded by strangers he could not fully observe, and he had started cycling the four miles to the dock regardless of weather. His crewmates had noticed the change in him. He had been passed over for a longer offshore contract because his captain, a man he respected, had told him plainly that he seemed unreliable and difficult to read. That conversation had shaken him more than almost anything since his return.

At home, Aleksander had developed the habit of lying awake in the early hours listening for sounds at the doors and windows. His wife, Marta, had tried to understand, but the distance between them had grown in ways neither of them had names for. It was Marta who finally made the appointment, after Aleksander told her one evening that he could not let himself feel anything soft or sad anymore — that whenever he felt emotionally open or unguarded, something in him slammed shut and turned hard. He had described it as feeling like exposure, like a gap in a wall.

What Aleksander fears most, sitting in the waiting room before his first therapy session, is that talking about it will put him back in that room. What he hopes, in a quieter part of himself, is that someone can explain why his body still believes it is there.
